Topics.Title: Introduction to the Standards Coverage View
Topics.Summary: An overview of PreseMaker's Standards Coverage view, including its current development status and the headline summary it provides about how well a course addresses its mapped standards.

Elements.Title: What Is the Standards Coverage View?
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view is a feature in PreseMaker that shows how well your course materials cover the standards you have mapped to it.
Elements.Notes: This view also evaluates whether each standard is addressed at the appropriate cognitive depth, going beyond simple alignment counts.

Items.Text: It provides a dedicated interface for reviewing all standards that have been mapped to a course.
Coverage is assessed across two dimensions: whether materials are aligned and whether the cognitive depth of those materials matches the standard.
The view is designed to give instructors an at-a-glance picture of potential gaps in their course design.

Elements.Title: Current Development Status
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view is a newer feature in PreseMaker and is currently labeled 'System in Development.'
Elements.Notes: This label signals that the feature may evolve over time, and users should be aware that its interface or functionality could change in future updates.

Items.Text: Like the Standards Library, the Standards Coverage view carries a 'System in Development' designation.
Users should expect the feature to be functional but potentially subject to refinement as the platform matures.
Despite its development status, the view already provides meaningful, actionable information about standards coverage.

Elements.Title: The Headline Summary
Elements.BodyText: At the top of the Standards Coverage view, a headline summarizes the overall state of standards coverage for the entire course.
Elements.Notes: For example, the headline might state what percentage of aligned standards are actually assessed and how many have a cognitive-depth gap, giving instructors an immediate sense of where attention is needed.

Items.Text: The headline aggregates data across all mapped standards into a concise, course-level summary.
It typically communicates two key figures: the percentage of standards that are assessed and the number of standards with a cognitive-depth gap.
This summary allows instructors to quickly prioritize which standards require further attention without reviewing every row individually.

Elements.Title: How Standards Are Displayed as Rows
Elements.BodyText: Each mapped standard appears as its own row in the Standards Coverage view, presenting several data points in a structured layout.
Elements.Notes: This row-based display makes it easy to scan across standards and compare their coverage details side by side.

Items.Text: Each row shows the standard's code and its full written statement for easy identification.
The row also displays the standard's cognitive (Bloom's) level alongside counts of aligned assignments, quiz items, and activities.
A Status field in each row indicates how thoroughly the standard has been addressed by course materials.

Elements.Title: The Role of the Status Field
Elements.BodyText: The Status field provides a tiered classification for each standard rather than a numeric score or percentage bar.
Elements.Notes: There are no numeric depth scores in this view; the tiers are the sole indicator of a standard's coverage state.

Items.Text: A standard may carry one of several status tiers: not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, or assessed.
'Not aligned' means nothing has been mapped to the standard, while 'not addressed' means the standard is mapped to the course but no assignment, quiz item, or activity is yet aligned to it.
'Practiced only' indicates that only activities are aligned, whereas 'assessed' means at least one assignment or quiz item is aligned to the standard.

Topics.Title: Reading the Coverage View Layout
Topics.Summary: Explains the information displayed for each mapped standard in the coverage view, including standard code, statement, Bloom's level, aligned content counts, and status indicators.

Elements.Title: The Coverage View Row Structure
Elements.BodyText: Each mapped standard appears as a single row in the coverage view, displaying several key pieces of information at a glance.
Elements.Notes: This row-based layout allows you to quickly scan all mapped standards and their coverage status without navigating away from the view.

Items.Text: Every row displays the standard's code and its full statement, giving you immediate context for what the standard requires.
The row also shows the standard's assigned Bloom's cognitive level, so you can see the depth of thinking the standard demands.
Counts of aligned assignments, quiz items, and activities are displayed, showing how many content pieces are connected to each standard.
A Status indicator rounds out each row, summarizing the overall coverage state of that standard.

Elements.Title: The Coverage Headline Summary
Elements.BodyText: A headline at the top of the coverage view provides an at-a-glance summary of how well all mapped standards are covered across the course.
Elements.Notes: For example, the headline might state what percentage of aligned standards are actually assessed and how many have a cognitive-depth gap.

Items.Text: The headline aggregates data across all mapped standards, giving you a course-wide picture without requiring row-by-row review.
It highlights two key metrics: the proportion of standards that are assessed and the count of standards with a cognitive-depth gap.

Elements.Title: Understanding the Tiered Status Indicators
Elements.BodyText: Each standard's Status field is drawn from a fixed set of tiers that describe the level of coverage that standard has received.
Elements.Notes: These tiers are qualitative labels, not numeric scores or percentage bars. There is no decimal or percentage value assigned to a standard's status.

Items.Text: Not aligned means nothing has been mapped to that standard at all.
Not addressed means the standard is mapped to the course, but no assignment, quiz item, or activity has been aligned to it yet.
Practiced only means the only content aligned to the standard is an activity — no assignments or quiz items are connected.
Assessed means at least one assignment or quiz item is aligned to the standard, confirming it has been formally assessed.

Elements.Title: What Counts as Assessment Versus Practice
Elements.BodyText: The coverage view makes a precise distinction between content that counts as assessment and content that counts as practice when determining a standard's status.
Elements.Notes: Misidentifying these categories leads to incorrect guidance — for instance, assignments should never be described as practice, and adding a quiz item to an already-assignment-aligned standard is not needed to achieve assessed status.

Items.Text: Assignments and quiz items both count as ASSESSMENT; a standard becomes assessed as soon as either one is aligned to it.
Activities are the only content type that counts as PRACTICE, which is why a standard shows practiced only when activities are its sole aligned content.
A standard already aligned to an assignment is already assessed — no additional quiz item is required to change its status.

Elements.Title: The Bloom's Level Column
Elements.BodyText: The coverage view displays the Bloom's cognitive level assigned to each standard, enabling comparison between what the standard demands and what aligned content delivers.
Elements.Notes: Bloom's levels represent a hierarchy of cognitive complexity, from lower-order recall to higher-order evaluation and creation.

Items.Text: Each standard row shows the Bloom's level that the standard itself requires, reflecting the cognitive depth expected of learners.
This column is the foundation for the cognitive-depth check, which compares the standard's level against the levels found in aligned learning outcomes.
Displaying the Bloom's level directly in the row helps you immediately identify which standards demand higher-order thinking.

Elements.Title: Aligned Content Counts per Standard
Elements.BodyText: The coverage view shows separate counts of assignments, quiz items, and activities aligned to each standard, giving you granular visibility into how coverage is distributed.
Elements.Notes: These counts help you identify standards that may be over-resourced in one content type but missing another, such as a standard with many activities but no assignments.

Items.Text: Assignment counts show how many formal assessment tasks have been aligned to the standard.
Quiz item counts reflect the number of individual quiz questions mapped to that standard.
Activity counts indicate how many practice-oriented tasks are aligned, which contribute to practice status but not assessed status.

Topics.Title: Understanding the Tiered Status System
Topics.Summary: Describes the four possible status tiers a standard can hold — not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, and assessed — and what conditions determine each tier.

Elements.Title: The Four Status Tiers Defined
Elements.BodyText: Every mapped standard is assigned one of four discrete status tiers that describe how thoroughly it is covered in the course.
Elements.Notes: These tiers are mutually exclusive and represent a progression from no coverage at all to full assessment.

Items.Text: The four tiers are: not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, and assessed.
A standard moves through these tiers as aligned materials are added to the course.
There are no numeric scores or percentage bars associated with a standard's status — only one of these four tier labels.

Elements.Title: Not Aligned Status
Elements.BodyText: A standard receives the 'not aligned' status when absolutely nothing in the course has been mapped to it.
Elements.Notes: This is the baseline state for any standard that exists in the standards library but has not yet been connected to the course.

Items.Text: No assignments, quiz items, or activities are associated with the standard in this state.
This status signals that the standard has not yet been incorporated into the course design at any level.

Elements.Title: Not Addressed Status
Elements.BodyText: A standard is 'not addressed' when it has been mapped to the course but no specific assignment, quiz item, or activity is aligned to it.
Elements.Notes: This distinction is important: the standard is acknowledged within the course's scope but lacks any concrete instructional or assessment material tied to it.

Items.Text: Mapping a standard to a course alone is not sufficient to move it out of this status.
At least one aligned assignment, quiz item, or activity must exist for the status to advance beyond 'not addressed.'
This tier highlights standards that are intended to be covered but have not yet been acted upon in course materials.

Elements.Title: Practiced Only Status
Elements.BodyText: A standard reaches 'practiced only' status when the sole aligned materials are activities — with no aligned assignments or quiz items present.
Elements.Notes: Activities are classified exclusively as practice, not assessment, which is why this tier is distinct from 'assessed.'

Items.Text: Only activities count as practice in the status system; assignments and quiz items are never considered practice.
A standard stuck at 'practiced only' indicates students engage with the content but are not formally assessed on it.
To advance this standard to 'assessed,' an aligned assignment or quiz item must be added.

Elements.Title: Assessed Status
Elements.BodyText: A standard achieves 'assessed' status as soon as at least one aligned assignment or aligned quiz item exists for it.
Elements.Notes: Both assignments and quiz items count as assessment — either one is sufficient to move a standard into the 'assessed' tier.

Items.Text: A standard does not need both an assignment and a quiz item to be assessed; one of either type is enough.
If a standard already has an aligned assignment, it is already assessed — adding a quiz item is not required to reach this tier.
Activities alone cannot produce 'assessed' status, regardless of how many are aligned to the standard.

Elements.Title: How Conditions Determine Tier Transitions
Elements.BodyText: The status tier a standard holds is directly determined by the type and presence of materials aligned to it, following a strict hierarchy.
Elements.Notes: Understanding these conditions prevents common errors such as treating assignments as practice or believing a quiz item is needed when an assignment already exists.

Items.Text: No alignment at all results in 'not aligned'; course-level mapping with no material alignment results in 'not addressed.'
Alignment to one or more activities only results in 'practiced only'; alignment to any assignment or quiz item results in 'assessed.'
The tier system is precise — the type of aligned material, not the quantity, determines whether a standard is practiced or assessed.

Topics.Title: Assessment vs. Practice: Key Distinctions
Topics.Summary: Clarifies the precise difference between what counts as assessment (assignments and quiz items) and what counts as practice (activities only), and how this affects a standard's status.

Elements.Title: The Two Categories: Assessment and Practice
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view divides aligned course materials into exactly two categories: assessment and practice. Understanding which category each material type belongs to is essential for interpreting a standard's status correctly.
Elements.Notes: These two categories are mutually exclusive and precisely defined — no material type crosses both categories.

Items.Text: Assignments and quiz items both belong to the ASSESSMENT category.
Only activities belong to the PRACTICE category.
Confusing an assignment with practice, or an activity with assessment, will lead to incorrect conclusions about a standard's status.

Elements.Title: What Makes a Standard 'Assessed'
Elements.BodyText: A standard reaches the 'assessed' status as soon as at least one aligned assignment or aligned quiz item exists in the course. No additional steps are required to move it into this status.
Elements.Notes: Because assignments already count as assessment, instructors should not be advised to add a quiz item to a standard that is already covered by an assignment in order to make it 'assessed' — it is already assessed.

Items.Text: A single aligned assignment is sufficient to push a standard's status to 'assessed.'
A single aligned quiz item is equally sufficient to reach 'assessed' status.
Having both an assignment and a quiz item aligned does not change the status beyond 'assessed' — it is already at the highest practice/assessment tier.

Elements.Title: What Makes a Standard 'Practiced Only'
Elements.BodyText: A standard shows a status of 'practiced only' when the sole aligned material is an activity — meaning no assignment or quiz item has been aligned to it yet.
Elements.Notes: This status signals that the standard has instructional engagement but lacks formal assessment. To move from 'practiced only' to 'assessed,' an instructor must align an assignment or quiz item, not another activity.

Items.Text: One or more aligned activities without any aligned assignment or quiz item results in 'practiced only.'
Adding more activities to a 'practiced only' standard will not change its status to 'assessed.'
To elevate the status, the instructor must align at least one assignment or one quiz item to that standard.

Elements.Title: The Lower Tiers: Not Aligned and Not Addressed
Elements.BodyText: Before a standard can be practiced or assessed, it must first be mapped and then have material aligned to it. Two lower-tier statuses reflect gaps at these earlier stages.
Elements.Notes: These statuses are distinct from 'practiced only' and 'assessed' and represent situations where no alignment work — not even an activity — has been completed.

Items.Text: 'Not aligned' means nothing at all has been mapped to that standard.
'Not addressed' means the standard is mapped to the course but no assignment, quiz item, or activity is yet aligned to it.
Both statuses indicate the standard is not contributing to coverage counts and require instructor action before assessment or practice status can be reached.

Elements.Title: How Status Affects Coverage Reporting
Elements.BodyText: The headline summary in the Standards Coverage view reflects how many standards are actually assessed, making the assessment-versus-practice distinction directly relevant to the reported coverage percentage.
Elements.Notes: A standard that is only 'practiced only' does not count toward the 'assessed' percentage in the headline summary, even if students are actively engaging with it through activities.

Items.Text: The headline reports the percentage of aligned standards that are assessed, not merely practiced.
Standards with 'practiced only,' 'not addressed,' or 'not aligned' statuses do not count toward the assessed percentage.
Accurate categorization of materials ensures that coverage reports reflect the true assessment footprint of the course.

Elements.Title: Common Misstatements to Avoid
Elements.BodyText: Two specific errors frequently arise when describing assessment versus practice distinctions, and both must be explicitly avoided when communicating about standards coverage.
Elements.Notes: These misstatements can cause instructors to take unnecessary or incorrect corrective actions in their course design.

Items.Text: Do not describe an assignment as 'practice' — assignments are assessment, not practice.

Do not instruct an instructor to add a quiz item in order to move a standard that is already covered by an assignment from 'practiced only' to 'assessed' — an aligned assignment already makes the standard 'assessed.'
Do not describe an activity as contributing to assessment status — activities only contribute to 'practiced only' status.

Topics.Title: How the Cognitive-Depth Check Works
Topics.Summary: Explains that PreseMaker compares a standard's Bloom's level against the highest Bloom's level of aligned learning outcomes, not materials, to determine whether a cognitive-depth gap exists.

Elements.Title: What a Cognitive-Depth Gap Is
Elements.BodyText: A cognitive-depth gap exists when a standard demands a higher Bloom's level than any of its aligned learning outcomes reach.
Elements.Notes: This gap is flagged automatically in the Standards Coverage view so instructors can see at a glance which standards are not being met at the required cognitive level.

Items.Text: Every standard carries a designated Bloom's taxonomic level indicating the depth of thinking it requires.
If no aligned learning outcome reaches that level, PreseMaker flags the standard as having a cognitive-depth gap.
The gap flag is a signal to revise or add learning outcomes, not to add more materials or assessments.

Elements.Title: The Comparison Is Between Standard and Learning Outcomes
Elements.BodyText: PreseMaker performs the cognitive-depth check by comparing a standard's Bloom's level against the learning outcomes aligned to that standard, not against the materials or assessments.
Elements.Notes: This distinction is critical: adding more assignments or quiz items does not resolve a cognitive-depth gap. Only raising the Bloom's level of aligned learning outcomes will close it.

Items.Text: The system looks at the highest Bloom's level found among all learning outcomes aligned to a given standard.
Materials such as assignments, quiz items, and activities are not part of the cognitive-depth calculation.
Conflating materials with learning outcomes in this check is a common misunderstanding that leads to incorrect corrective action.

Elements.Title: The Role of Learning Outcomes in the Check
Elements.BodyText: Learning outcomes serve as the sole reference point for determining whether a standard's cognitive depth is being met.
Elements.Notes: Each learning outcome has its own Bloom's level, and PreseMaker uses the highest of those levels across all outcomes aligned to a standard as the comparison value.

Items.Text: A single high-level learning outcome can satisfy the cognitive-depth requirement even if other aligned outcomes are at lower levels.
PreseMaker uses the highest Bloom's level among aligned outcomes, so the comparison is always against the best-case outcome depth.
If no learning outcomes are aligned to a standard, a cognitive-depth gap will exist by default regardless of what materials are present.

Elements.Title: How the Comparison Determines a Gap
Elements.BodyText: The check applies a straightforward rule: if the standard's Bloom's level exceeds the highest Bloom's level of its aligned learning outcomes, a gap is flagged.
Elements.Notes: For example, if a standard is at the Evaluate level but the highest aligned learning outcome is at the Apply level, PreseMaker identifies this as a cognitive-depth gap.

Items.Text: When the standard's level equals or is lower than the highest aligned outcome level, no gap is flagged.
When the standard's level is higher than the highest aligned outcome level, the coverage view marks that standard with a cognitive-depth gap.
This binary comparison means the gap either exists or it does not; there is no partial or percentage-based depth score.

Elements.Title: What the Cognitive-Depth Check Does Not Evaluate
Elements.BodyText: The cognitive-depth check is deliberately scoped to learning outcomes only and does not assess the Bloom's levels of assignments, quiz items, or activities.
Elements.Notes: Keeping the check focused on learning outcomes ensures consistency, since learning outcomes are the formal statements of intended cognitive achievement rather than delivery mechanisms.

Items.Text: Adding or removing assignments, quiz items, or activities has no effect on whether a cognitive-depth gap is flagged.
The check does not produce a numeric depth score or a percentage; it simply determines whether a gap exists.
Resolving a cognitive-depth gap requires action at the learning-outcome level, such as rewriting an outcome to a higher Bloom's level or aligning a new outcome at the required level.

Topics.Title: Identifying and Addressing Cognitive-Depth Gaps
Topics.Summary: Guides learners in interpreting cognitive-depth flags in the coverage view and understanding how to strengthen course design where learning outcomes fall short of the depth a standard demands.

Elements.Title: What a Cognitive-Depth Gap Means
Elements.BodyText: A cognitive-depth gap is flagged when a standard demands a higher Bloom's level than any learning outcome aligned to that standard achieves.
Elements.Notes: For example, if a standard requires 'Evaluate' (Bloom's Level 5) but all aligned learning outcomes are written at the 'Understand' level, the system flags a depth gap for that standard.

Items.Text: Each standard carries a designated Bloom's cognitive level that reflects the depth of thinking it requires.
PreseMaker compares the standard's Bloom's level against the highest Bloom's level found among its aligned learning outcomes.
If no aligned learning outcome reaches the standard's required level, the coverage view flags a cognitive-depth gap for that standard.
This flag signals a design problem at the outcome level, not necessarily a missing assignment or activity.

Elements.Title: Where to Find Cognitive-Depth Flags in the Coverage View
Elements.BodyText: The Standards Coverage view displays each mapped standard as a row, making it straightforward to locate which standards carry a cognitive-depth gap.
Elements.Notes: A headline summary at the top of the coverage view indicates how many standards have a cognitive-depth gap across the entire course, giving a quick overall picture before drilling into individual rows.

Items.Text: Each row shows the standard's code, statement, and its designated Bloom's cognitive level alongside alignment counts.
The headline summary reports both the percentage of standards that are assessed and how many have a cognitive-depth gap.
Rows flagged with a depth gap can be identified and prioritized for revision directly within this view.

Elements.Title: Understanding What the Depth Check Reads
Elements.BodyText: The cognitive-depth check evaluates learning outcomes aligned to a standard, not the assignments, quiz items, or activities themselves.
Elements.Notes: This is a critical distinction: adding more assessments or activities will not resolve a cognitive-depth gap. The fix must happen at the learning outcome level.

Items.Text: The system reads the Bloom's level of each learning outcome aligned to the standard and identifies the highest level among them.
Materials such as assignments, quizzes, and activities are not analyzed for cognitive depth in this check.
To resolve a depth gap, learners must revise or add learning outcomes that reach or exceed the standard's required Bloom's level.

Elements.Title: Interpreting the Status Tiers Alongside Depth Gaps
Elements.BodyText: A standard's Status tier and its cognitive-depth flag are separate indicators that together describe the completeness and depth of coverage.
Elements.Notes: A standard can be 'assessed' (meaning an assignment or quiz item is aligned) and still carry a cognitive-depth gap if its learning outcomes do not reach the required Bloom's level.

Items.Text: Status tiers — not aligned, not addressed, practiced only, and assessed — reflect whether and how materials are linked to the standard.
A cognitive-depth gap can coexist with any status tier, including 'assessed,' because depth is measured against outcomes, not materials.
Addressing a depth gap requires action on learning outcomes even when the status tier already shows the standard is assessed.

Elements.Title: Strategies for Strengthening Learning Outcomes to Close Depth Gaps
Elements.BodyText: Closing a cognitive-depth gap requires rewriting existing learning outcomes or adding new ones that reflect the Bloom's level the standard demands.
Elements.Notes: Using Bloom's taxonomy verb lists can help when rewriting outcomes — for instance, replacing 'identify' (Remember) with 'critique' or 'evaluate' when a standard requires evaluative thinking.

Items.Text: Review the Bloom's level of the flagged standard and compare it directly to the verb choices in your current aligned learning outcomes.
Revise outcome language to use verbs that correspond to the required cognitive level, such as moving from 'describe' to 'analyze' or 'evaluate.'
Adding a new learning outcome at the appropriate depth is also valid when existing outcomes cannot be easily elevated.
After revising outcomes, revisit the coverage view to confirm the flag has been resolved.

Elements.Title: Avoiding Common Misreads When Addressing Depth Gaps
Elements.BodyText: Learners sometimes confuse the cognitive-depth gap with a coverage gap and attempt to fix it by adding assessments or activities rather than revising outcomes.
Elements.Notes: Adding a quiz item moves a standard from 'practiced only' to 'assessed,' but it does not close a cognitive-depth gap — that requires outcome-level changes.

Items.Text: Adding assignments or quiz items addresses assessment coverage but does not influence the cognitive-depth check.
Adding activities contributes to practice coverage but similarly has no effect on the depth flag.
The only lever for resolving a cognitive-depth gap is the Bloom's level of the learning outcomes aligned to the standard.
Always distinguish between a status-tier problem (no aligned materials) and a depth problem (outcomes not reaching the required level) before taking corrective action.
